## Problem 1 - Birthday Paradox Findings
The birthday paradox is the notion that for a randomly selected group of individuals, there is ~51% chance that at least two people in the group share the same birthday. Lets find out more about this!

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
# Make a function for the birthday paradox itself.
birthday_pardox = function(n) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  length(birthdays) > length(unique(birthdays))
}


# Run the function 10,000 times (Group Size: 2-50)
paradox_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    n = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) %>% 
  mutate(result 
         = map_lgl(n, birthday_pardox)) %>% 
  group_by(n) %>% 
  summarize(prob = mean(result))


# Data viz of birthday paradox!
paradox_results_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = prob)) +
  geom_line(color = "#e63919", linewidth = 1.5) + 
  geom_point(color = "#ffb711", size = 2) +       
  labs(
    title = "The Birthday Paradox",
    subtitle = "Based on 10,000 Simulations for Groups of 2-50",
    x = "Group Size (N)",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthday"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1d3551"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#457b9a")
  )
```


#### Figure 1 Interpretation
Guided by the Birthday Paradox, this figure highlights that as the size of a group increases, the probability of at least two individuals sharing a birthday increases (not linear manner). This aligns with our understanding because the number of possible pairs of individuals grows quickly rather than linearly with group size.
